title: External GET and POST APIs
summary: Consume external APIs with DTOs, explicit timeouts, and clear failure handling.

sources.title: Engineering Digest: Master External API Integration in Spring Boot: A Step-by-Step Guide
Engineering Digest: Spring Boot Tutorial: How to Consume External POST APIs Effectively

richText: Choose the request from the API contract
An external API belongs to another service. Your Spring application sends an HTTP request and reads its response.

Use GET to read a resource, such as weather for a city. Use POST when the provider requires a request body or performs an action. Follow the provider contract instead of choosing the method from the Java method name.
Keep the provider URL, credentials, and request logic in a service. A controller should call that service rather than build provider requests itself.
A DTO is a data transfer object. Define request and response fields from the provider JSON. Keep provider DTOs separate from database entities.
The course repository uses RestTemplate. These examples use Spring Boot 3.2+ with Spring Framework 6.1+ and Java 17. Earlier Spring versions do not provide RestClient.
Configure one reusable HTTP client
RestClient waits for the response. Use it for a normal blocking request flow. WebClient fits a reactive application or streamed responses.
A connect timeout limits connection setup. A read timeout limits waiting for the response. This example uses the JDK HTTP client and explicit limits.
api.base-url is application configuration. Use a fixed trusted provider URL. Do not let users choose arbitrary target hosts.
Read a resource and submit JSON
For this illustrative provider, GET /weather?city=Pune returns {"city":"Pune","temperatureC":26.0}. POST /analyses accepts text and returns {"label":"POSITIVE"}.
URI parameters encode input. contentType declares the sent body format. The response DTO tells Spring how to read the returned JSON.
Handle failures at the boundary
retrieve throws for HTTP 4xx and 5xx by default. Distinguish bad credentials, rate limits, unavailable services, invalid responses, and timeouts.
Check for an empty body before reading DTO fields. Use toEntity when response status or headers are needed.
Retry only failures that can recover. A timed-out POST may already have completed. Retry an action only with a provider-supported idempotency key or another duplicate-prevention contract.
Keep API keys in environment configuration and the provider-required authentication header. Avoid logging credentials or private request bodies.
